items.title: ChainDrop supply chain compromise: Anatomy of a self-propagating worm
items.summary:
In this article Attack chain overview Mitigation and protection guidance Indicators of compromise (IOC) Microsoft Defender XDR detections Advanced hunting queries Learn more Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a large-scale npm supply chain attack affecting more than 400 packages across multiple unrelated publishers, including packages associated with major enterprise software ecosystems such as keyv, flat-cache, cache-manager, and others. The malicious releases contain a Mini Shai-Hulud variant, a self-propagating credential-stealing worm delivered through a large, heavily obfuscated Bun-based JavaScript payload. The malware typically executes automatically through an npm preinstall lifecycle hook before package installation completes. Once executed, the malware searches developer workstations and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) environments for npm, GitHub, cloud, and infrastructure credentials. It uses recovered identities to authenticate to npm, GitHub, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Kubernetes, and HashiCorp Vault, enabling it to enumerate packages, repositories, workflow secrets, cloud parameters, and secret-store values. Collected data is encrypted and transmitted through an attacker-controlled HTTPS endpoint, with GitHub repositories serving as a fallback exfiltration channel. The payload’s most significant capability is automated propagation. After obtaining an npm publishing token, it enumerates packages available to the compromised identity, downloads their latest tarballs, inserts the malware and setup loader, adds a preinstall hook, increments the patch version, and republishes the modified packages. The malware can also use stolen GitHub credentials to inject Claude and Visual Studio Code configuration files into repositories, establishing persistence and creating an additional developer-to-developer infection path. In this blog, we’re sharing our analysis of this supply chain attack, along with protection, detection, amd hunting guidance. Organizations that installed an affected package with lifecycle scripts enabled should treat the associated developer workstation or build runner as potentially compromised. Investigations should prioritize credentials accessible to the affected identity, unauthorized npm releases, unexpected repository or workflow modifications, suspicious cloud and secret-store access, and artifacts produced by affected build systems. Organizations should revoke and rotate exposed credentials from a known-clean environment and rebuild affected systems and downstream artifacts from trusted sources. Attack chain overview The campaign appeared as a rapid sequence of unauthorized patch releases across more than 400 npm packages maintained by otherwise unrelated publishers. Many malicious versions had no corresponding source-code commit, pull request, tag, or legitimate release, indicating that the attackers modified and published package tarballs directly rather than compromising each public source repository. Affected releases typically added a preinstall lifecycle script that launched a malicious file, setup.mjs, contained within the package, which launched the large, obfuscated Bun JavaScript bundle included in the package. Because npm runs preinstall scripts before installation completes, the payload could execute on developer workstations and build runners before application tests or conventional security checks began. After execution, the malware performs the following actions: Determines whether it is running on a developer workstation or in a CI/CD environment. On workstations, it detaches itself to continue after installation; on CI/CD systems, it remains in the active job to access workflow secrets, runner credentials, and OpenID Connect (OIDC) publishing permissions. Both paths could support further package or repository propagation when suitable credentials are found. Collects credentials from local files, environment variables, command-line tools, and GitHub Actions runner memory. Authenticates to npm, GitHub, AWS, Kubernetes, and HashiCorp Vault to enumerate additional accessible resources and secrets. Encrypts and exfiltrates collected data through an HTTPS channel, using GitHub repositories as a fallback. Uses recovered npm publishing access to modify and republish additional packages. Uses GitHub credentials to inject files into Claude and Visual Studio Code configurations across repository branches for persistence. The payload’s  package-propagation routine downloads each publisher’s latest release, inserts itself, increments the patch version, and publishes the resulting archive. This mechanism can rapidly transform one compromised npm identity into many malicious package releases. Figure 1. Attack chain. 0. Initial publisher access Evidence points towards stolen maintainer credentials as the attack vector for initial compromise. Later propagation used stolen npm publishing tokens and, in targeted workflows, GitHub Actions OIDC publishing access. 1. Payload startup and background execution The malicious npm package uses a lifecycle hook to launch its bundle. During preflight, the payload checks the environment, exits on Russian-language systems, avoids duplicate instances, and starts a detached copy in the background on developer systems. Figure 2. Platform identification and execution. In CI environments, the payload remains attached so it can access credentials available to the active build job. 2. Initial credential discovery The payload first collects information that is immediately available from the local system, shell, and GitHub Actions runner. Figure 3. Credential discovery. The shell collector attempts to obtain the GitHub CLI token and captures the values of all process environment variables. The filesystem collector searches credential files, shell histories, cloud configuration, Secure Shell (SSH) keys, and other sensitive locations. 3. Cloud and secret store enumeration The recovered code then creates dedicated collectors for cloud and infrastructure services. Figure 4. Credential enumeration. These modules do not merely scan files for token patterns; they use available credentials to call service APIs, verify access, and retrieve additional secrets permitted to those identities. The following snippet shows the authentication attempt made using the found credentials: Figure 5. Credential validation. 4 . GitHub credential theft and enumeration Discovered GitHub tokens are validated before being used for additional collection or repository access. Figure 6. GitHub credential collector. The payload checks token scopes, enumerates writable repositories, and identifies repositories where workflow execution could expose additional secrets. 6 . GitHub Actions OIDC abuse The payload also contains a targeted publishing path for GitHub Actions workflows configured as npm trusted publishers. Figure 7. Re-publishing package using GitHub OIDC token. Packages published through this route can carry valid provenance because the publication originates from a legitimate workflow identity. 7. Exfiltration and fallback Collected results are serialized as JSON, gzip-compressed, and encrypted with a randomly generated AES-256-GCM using a randomly generated 32-byte key and 12-byte initialization vector (IV). The AES key is then encrypted with the attacker’s RSA public key using RSA-OAEP-SHA256. The payload first attempts delivery through an attacker-controlled dynamic HTTPS endpoint. The active domain can change through on-chain contract (0xE1f2395ee43e45A1556EC6438a88c31B83493103, selector 0x53ed5143) or, as a fallback, from a cryptographically verified signed GitHub commit (Signed fallback marker: thebeautifulmarchoftime). If that channel is unavailable, it creates a public GitHub repository with the description Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again . Encrypted results are committed as files such as: results- - .json . At the time of analysis, the live contract returns npm-cache[.]com . Earlier candidates include pypi-get[.]com and js-mirror[.]com . Figure 8. Exfiltrating stolen information. In one fallback path, a stolen GitHub token is added separately using double Base64 encoding. This token field is encoded, not encrypted. 8. Repository persistence and secondary spread The payload can use stolen GitHub credentials to inject the malware and supporting setup files into eligible repository branches. The recovered code targets Claude and Visual Studio Code configuration paths, including . claude/settings.json , .claude/setup.mjs , .vscode/tasks.json , and .vscode/setup.mjs . These changes create a secondary infection route: future Claude or Visual Studio Code activity can restart the payload even after the original npm installation has completed. In a conditional GitHub fallback path, the payload also attempts to install a token-monitor component that maintains credential access and contains a destructive handler if the monitored token is revoked. Figure 9. Injecting the malicious code into development ecosystems. 9. Worm behavior: Package modification and publication The npm tokens found in collected data are checked for package-write permission and two-factor authentication (2FA)-bypass capability. Figure 10. Republishing the package using stolen NPM token. Figure 11. Malicious update to existing package and republishing. The propagation routine downloads a package’s latest tarball, copies the current malware bundle into it, adds a loader, and replaces its lifecycle scripts. This creates the worm-like propagation pattern: one stolen token can produce malicious patch releases across every package available to that publisher. This also explains why malicious releases frequently appeared as an otherwise ordinary patch-version increment without corresponding source commits or pull requests. Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Update npm CLI to npm CLI v 12 and use the npm CLI min-release-age feature. Review dependency trees, lockfiles, artifact repositories, and CI caches for the five compromised versions, including transitive references. Pin known-good package versions. Purge npm and yarn caches on affected developer endpoints and build hosts, especially if the compromised tarballs were written into shared CI caches. Rotate credentials and secrets from a clean host if a build system or workstation imported a compromised version, because second-stage execution can expose tokens and compromise build integrity. Ensure that Microsoft Defender Antivirus cloud-delivered protection, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry, Microsoft Defender for Containers, and Microsoft Defender XDR investigation workflows are enabled across developer and CI assets. Organizations that produce software artifacts should also review their own release hardening because this incident appears consistent with CI/CD pipeline abuse through GitHub Actions OIDC publishing. Defenders should review token scopes, workflow approvals, protected environments, release provenance, and anomaly detection around automated package publication. Supply chain response cannot stop at host triage; it must also include verification that the release process itself has not been subverted. After remediation, validate recovery deliberately. Rebuild affected projects from a known-good dependency baseline, confirm that compromised hashes are absent from package caches and artifact stores, and review endpoint telemetry for any lingering NodeJS directory artifacts such as Math_Symbol.js , Math_init.js ,  or names similar to math_ .js , or suspicious node child processes. For development organizations that share base images or golden build runners, rebuild those images as well so future jobs do not silently inherit poisoned caches or post-compromise persistence. Figure 3. Credential discovery.

The shell collector attempts to obtain the GitHub CLI token and captures the values of all process environment variables. The filesystem collector searches credential files, shell histories, cloud configuration, Secure Shell (SSH) keys, and other sensitive locations.

The npm tokens found in collected data are checked for package-write permission and two-factor authentication (2FA)-bypass capability.

  • Purge npm and yarn caches on affected developer endpoints and build hosts, especially if the compromised tarballs were written into shared CI caches.

Supply chain response cannot stop at host triage; it must also include verification that the release process itself has not been subverted.
  • After remediation, validate recovery deliberately. items.summary_html:
This is a big release with lots of bare-metal goodness. The Barebone agent— written in Rust and embedding the GumJS devkit—previously supported only XNU. It can now also run in the Linux kernel, where a small C shim provides the kernel glue.

The agent is packaged as a .ko: load it with insmod, then exchange length-prefixed GVariant messages through /dev/frida. Configure the Barebone backend to use this transport, and run frida-server --device=barebone on the device. Here it is running on my Pixel 6 Pro:

Full changelog:

  • gumjs: Fix a detach hang when a native fault inside JS is recovered by a later handler. We now rebalance the Interceptor transaction when the thread survives, instead of ending it twice. Kudos to @pandasauce for reporting the issue and helping track it down.
  • arm64: Detect branches into the range being relocated, preventing Interceptor from rewriting a branch so that it lands in the middle of its own redirect patch. Thanks to @WHW0x455 for this fix.
  • python: Fix the linker_notifier_offsets keyword argument to attach(), restore the default port for Script.enable_debugger(), and reinstate marshalling of certificate options for remote devices and related APIs.
  • barebone: Add support for running the agent as a Linux kernel module. The agent now starts inside the target as a .ko, exposes a character device for transport, and can be reached through a regular frida-server --device=barebone instance.
  • deps: Add a soft-float bare-metal SDK comprising picolibc and compiler-rt. This gives the none-arm64-softfloat flavour a libc and runtime that agree on passing floating-point values through general-purpose registers.
  • deps: Build the soft-float SDK in CI, check for published bundles before spending time installing a toolchain, keep libc headers out of devkit headers, use the SDK as the sysroot, and ensure configure-time link checks resolve libc correctly.
  • deps: Bump GLib, libffi, and QuickJS for freestanding fixes, vector assembler directive fixes, the precedence-climbing parser, and the corresponding x18 fix.
  • arm64: Avoid FP and SIMD code on soft-float targets by using scalar fallbacks for memcpy, pointer scanning, and Interceptor’s register shuffling.
  • gumjs: Bound the QuickJS stack on bare metal, re-enabling its stack check so the parser stops before exhausting the small stacks such hosts may provide.

items.title: Micropatches released for Windows Internet Key Exchange Service Extensions RCE (CVE-2026-33824)
items.summary:
April 2026 Windows Updates brought a patch for CVE-2026-33824, a remote code execution vulnerability in Windows IKE Extension, allowing an unauthorized attacker in the network to cause memory corruption in a privileged service on another computer in the network and potentially execute privileged arbitrary code there.
The vulnerability was found internally by Microsoft WARP & MORSE team. We recreated a POC from the official patch, which allowed us to reproduce the issue and create patches for legacy Windows systems.

The Vulnerability 
This is a pre-authentication double free in ikeext.dll, the module behind the "IKE and AuthIP IPsec Keying Modules" service, which runs as Local System inside a svchost.exe. The flaw is in function IkeReinjectReassembledPacket, on the IKEv2 fragment reassembly path. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach UDP 500/4500 on a host that acts as an IKEv2 responder can free the same heap block twice, resulting inpotentially exploitable memory corruption.

items.title: When Attackers Hijack Your Inbox: Detecting Mailbox Forwarding Rules with Microsoft Defender XDR
items.summary: Business Email Compromise (BEC) attacks continue to be one of the most common and costly cyber threats for organizations today. Once attackers gain access to a user’s Microsoft 365 account, whether through phishing, stolen credentials, or session hijacking, they often seek ways to maintain long-term visibility into the victim’s mailbox without repeatedly signing in. One of the simplest and most effective persistence techniques is creating a mailbox forwarding rule that silently sends copies of emails to an attacker-controlled account. Because mailbox forwarding rules are legitimate Exchange Online features, they can easily blend in with normal user activities. A forwarding rule created for an executive, finance employee, or legal team member may go unnoticed for weeks or even months, allowing attackers to silently monitor conversations, intercept sensitive information, and continue collecting intelligence without repeatedly signing in to the compromised account. Fortunately, these attacker activities are not invisible. Microsoft Purview Audit captures mailbox operations, including the creation of forwarding rules, and these audit events are also available in Microsoft Defender XDR Advanced Hunting. This allows security teams to proactively hunt for suspicious mailbox activities and create custom detection rules that can automatically alert on malicious behavior. In this article, we’ll explore how to leverage Microsoft Purview Audit events in Defender XDR Advanced Hunting to detect suspicious mailbox forwarding rules and build increasingly sophisticated detections through telemetry correlation. We’ll start with simple hunting queries before progressing to more advanced detection scenarios that correlate mailbox activity with identity and security alert telemetry to uncover potential Business Email Compromise attacks. Specifically, we’ll cover how to: · Discover newly created mailbox forwarding rules across the tenant. · Detect forwarding rules created for high-value or high-risk users. · Identify multiple user mailboxes forwarding to the same email address. · Detect forwarding rules that forward email to suspicious or unapproved external domains. · Correlate suspicious Microsoft Entra ID sign-ins with subsequent mailbox forwarding rule creation. · Correlate Defender XDR security alerts with mailbox forwarding rules created shortly afterward to identify potential post-compromise persistence. By the end of this article, you’ll have a collection of practical KQL queries that can be used for proactive threat hunting or converted into custom detection rules. Together, they help your security team identify and respond to Business Email Compromise attacks more quickly and effectively. A Quick Introduction to Purview Audit Log Microsoft Purview Audit captures user and administrator actions across Microsoft 365 services, including Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, Entra ID, Microsoft Copilot, Security Copilot, and more. These audit events log who did what, where, and when . They serve as a trusted source for security investigations, compliance reporting, legal discovery, and threat hunting. For mailbox investigations, Microsoft Purview Audit records Exchange Online operations such as creating, modifying, and deleting inbox rules, which include mailbox forwarding rules. These events can be searched directly from the Microsoft Purview Audit portal or from the integrated audit experience in Microsoft Defender XDR ( https://security.microsoft.com/auditlogsearch ). As an example, the screenshot below shows an audit search configured to find inbox rule events. The detailed audit record for one of the returned events is shown below: While the Purview Audit portal is useful for reviewing individual events, one of the lesser-known capabilities of Defender XDR is that the same audit events are also available in Advanced Hunting. This allows you to investigate mailbox activity alongside endpoint, identity, email, cloud application, and security alert telemetry within a single hunting experience. More importantly, it enables correlation of mailbox events with other signals to build behavioral detections that would be difficult to achieve using audit logs alone. As an example, the following KQL query returns a summary of inbox rule creation events observed in the last 15 days. // This query returns a summary of inbox rule creation events in the last 15 days CloudAppEvents | where ActionType == "New-InboxRule" and Timestamp > ago (15d) | extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData) | extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId) | project Timestamp, ActionType, Application, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP | sort by Timestamp asc A portion of the data returned by the query is shown in the following screenshot: Detecting Mailbox Forwarding Rules Not all inbox rules are suspicious. Users frequently create rules to organize their inboxes, move messages into folders, or automatically categorize incoming email. From a security perspective, however, mailbox forwarding rules deserve special attention because they are commonly used by attackers to establish persistence after compromising an account. To demonstrate how these activities are captured in Microsoft Purview Audit, I set up three different mailbox forwarding scenarios in a test tenant. The events generated by these scenarios serve as the data queried by the KQL queries presented throughout this article. Using known events makes it easier to understand how each query works and how to interpret its results. On June 28, 2026, at 3:55 PM MT , I created an inbox rule named “Forward Mail to Personal Account” that forwards messages to bxx@yahoo.com. The rule configuration is shown below. On June 28, 2026, at 11:03 PM MT, I deleted this mail forwarding rule. On June 28, 2026, at 11:05 PM MT , I created a mailbox redirect rule that redirects messages to my personal email account at bxx@yahoo.com. Unlike the “Forward to” feature, where recipients can see that the message was forwarded by me, the “Redirect to” option preserves the original sender information, making the email appear to come directly from the original sender. The following screenshot shows the inbox redirect rule configuration. In addition to creating an inbox rule, Outlook also allows you to enable mailbox forwarding, which automatically forwards all incoming messages to another email address. On June 28, 2026, at 10:09 PM MT , I enabled mailbox forwarding by turning on “Enable forwarding” and configured all incoming messages to be forwarded to my personal Yahoo account, as shown in the following screenshot. Unlike inbox rules, mailbox forwarding configured this way does not have a rule name. As I configured the different email forwarding settings, these activities were captured by Microsoft Purview Audit and became available in Defender Advanced Hunting in near real time. The following KQL query lists various mailbox forwarding rule creation events, including the three scenarios just described: // This query lists mailbox forwarding rule creation events CloudAppEvents | where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox") | extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData) | extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId) | extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters) | mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue) | extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue) | extend ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName, Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name), ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value) | where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" | where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@" | project Timestamp, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP | sort by Timestamp asc As shown in the next screen capture, the query successfully identifies the three different types of mailbox forwarding scenarios that were just discussed. Security Use Cases: Turning Mailbox Forwarding Telemetry into Actionable Detections Detecting mailbox forwarding rules is a good starting point. The real power comes from connecting the dots across Microsoft Defender XDR telemetry to uncover attack patterns that may otherwise go unnoticed. By correlating mailbox forwarding activity with user risk, external destinations, identity signals, and existing security alerts, security teams can transform simple audit events into powerful behavioral detections. Use Case 1: Detecting and Alerting on Mailbox Forwarding Rules Created for High-Risk Users Attackers don’t always target random mailboxes. They often prioritize accounts with access to valuable information, such as executives, finance teams, legal departments, HR personnel, and security leaders. By creating mailbox forwarding rules on these high-value accounts, attackers can quietly monitor sensitive communications and collect intelligence while remaining unnoticed. Security teams can reduce this risk by prioritizing mailbox forwarding activities involving high-risk users. By adding a user-based filter, the mailbox forwarding query introduced earlier can be easily customized to focus only on specific accounts that require additional monitoring. For example, the following filter limits the query to three predefined high-risk users: | where User has_any ("axx@mycompany.com", "bxx@mycompany.com", "cxx@mycompany.com") In a production environment, this list can be customized based on organization’s privileged accounts, executive users, sensitive business roles, or other identities requiring enhanced monitoring. The complete updated query, including the high-risk user filter, is shown below: // This query detects mailbox forwarding rules created for high-risk users CloudAppEvents | where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox") | extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData) | extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId) | where User has_any ("axx@mycompany.com", "bxx@ mycompany.com", "cxx@mycompany.com") | extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters) | mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue) | extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue) | extend ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName, Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name), ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value) | where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" | where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@" | project Timestamp, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP | sort by Timestamp asc Operationalizing Threat Hunting with Custom Detection Rules Threat hunting queries are valuable for investigating suspicious activity, but security teams can take it a step further by converting these queries into custom detection rules. This allows Microsoft Defender XDR to continuously run the KQL query in the background and automatically generate an alert when matching activity is detected. As shown below, the “Create detection rule” option (highlighted in the red box) allows you to turn any hunting query into an automated detection. The next screenshot shows the configuration experience for creating the custom detection rule. Use Case 2: Detecting Multiple Mailboxes Forwarding to the Same External Email Address A single mailbox forwarding rule set to an external address may be legitimate. However, multiple user mailboxes forwarding to the same external email address can be suspicious. This pattern may indicate a large-scale compromise, insider activity, or an attacker systematically collecting sensitive communications from multiple users. KQL makes it easy to uncover this type of activity by aggregating mailbox forwarding events. The following query detects when three or more user mailboxes are configured to forward email to the same external email address. // This query finds multiple mailboxes forwarding to the same external recipient CloudAppEvents | where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox") | extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData) | extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId) | extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters) | mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue) | extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue) | extend ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName, Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name), ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value) | where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" | where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@" and ForwardingEmailAddress !endswith "@mycompany.com" // Change from mycompany.com to your own domain | summarize Users = make_set(User), UserCount = dcount(User), RuleNames = make_set(ForwardingRuleName) by ForwardingEmailAddress | where UserCount >= 3 In this query, the threshold is controlled by the following filter: | where UserCount >= 3 You can easily adjust this value to suit your environment. Additionally, to reduce noise, this query also excludes your organization’s email domain by using the following filter: ForwardingEmailAddress !endswith "@mycompany.com" Don’t forget to replace @mycompany.com with your organization’s email domain so the query focuses only on mail forwarded to external recipients. Use Case 3: Detecting Mailbox Forwarding Rules to Specific External Domains Security analysts are often interested in identifying unauthorized or suspicious email forwarding to external email services such as Gmail, Yahoo, and other personal email providers. This is more than just a compliance concern; these services are also common destinations for mailbox forwarding rules created by attackers. Monitoring forwarding activity to these domains provides a simple but effective way to detect potential Business Email Compromise and unauthorized data exfiltration. The following query identifies mailbox forwarding rules configured to a predefined list of external domains, including Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook.com, and Proton Mail. // This query finds mailbox forwarding rules set to specific external domains CloudAppEvents | where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox") | extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData) | extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId) | extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters) | mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue) | extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue) | extend ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName, Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name), ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value) | where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" | where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@" | where ForwardingEmailAddress has_any ("gmail.com", "yahoo.com", "outlook.com", "proton.me") // Customize this list by adding or removing external domains of interest | project Timestamp, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP | sort by Timestamp asc Note, the external domain list in the KQL query is fully customizable. You can update the query filter by adding or removing domains based on the email services or destinations that are most relevant to your organization’s security monitoring needs. Use Case 4: One Event is Interesting. Two Related Events Tell a Story. Correlating Suspicious Sign-ins with Mailbox Forwarding Rules A mailbox forwarding rule by itself may not be enough to indicate malicious activity. However, when it is created shortly after a suspicious sign-in, the story becomes much more compelling. Instead of investigating mailbox activity in isolation, you can correlate mailbox forwarding telemetry with suspicious Microsoft Entra ID sign-in events to uncover post-compromise persistence commonly seen in Business Email Compromise attacks. The EntraIdSignInEvents table in Defender Advanced Hunting contains Microsoft Entra ID sign-in events, including sign-ins to Microsoft 365 and other applications authenticated through Entra ID. It also provides additional identity context, such as device name, IP address, geographic location, and session details. This allows the identification of unusual or suspicious sign-in activity. By combining this information with mailbox forwarding events, security teams can identify suspicious behavioral sequences rather than isolated events. For example, the user, as shown below, normally signs in from Denver, Colorado using a registered device named FamilyPC1 . This user consistently accesses resources through the Microsoft Edge browser with the same user agent. However, as seen from the screenshot below, one sign-in event stands out. It originates from Cheyenne, Wyoming , using a different browser, is not associated with a registered device, and contains no user agent information. This suspicious sign-in becomes even more interesting when it is followed by a mailbox forwarding event involving the same user account. The following KQL query correlates such suspicious Entra ID sign-ins with subsequent mailbox forwarding rule creation to identify those potential attack patterns. // This query identifies suspicious sign-in followed by the creation of a mail forwarding rule let SuspiciousSignIns = EntraIdSignInEvents | where State != "Colorado" | where Application == "Office 365 Exchange Online" | extend User = AccountUpn, SignInTime = Timestamp, UserSignInIP = IPAddress | project SignInTime, User, UserSignInIP, Country, State, City, Application, LogonType, DeviceName, OSPlatform, DeviceTrustType, IsManaged, Browser, UserAgent; let MailForwarding = CloudAppEvents | where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox") | extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData) | extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId), ForwardTime = Timestamp | extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters) | mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue) | extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue) | extend ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName, Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name), ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value) | where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" | where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@" | project ForwardTime, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP; SuspiciousSignIns | join kind=inner MailForwarding on User | where ForwardTime between (SignInTime .. SignInTime + 1d) | project SignInTime, ForwardTime, TimeToForwardRule = ForwardTime - SignInTime, User, UserSignInIP, Country, State, City, Application, LogonType, DeviceName, OSPlatform, DeviceTrustType, IsManaged, Browser, UserAgent, ActionType, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress | sort by SignInTime asc, ForwardTime asc Using the events from the previous three test scenarios along with the suspicious Entra ID sign-in discussed earlier, this query connects the dots across multiple security signals and brings the entire attack sequence together in a single query output. It identifies an unusual sign-in from Wyoming, followed by the creation of multiple mailbox forwarding rules, allowing analysts to see the related activities and timeline in one view. The next two screenshots highlight different portions of the KQL query output. The first screenshot shows the beginning of the results, while the second displays a later section of the output. This KQL query uses geographic deviation as the signal to identify potentially suspicious sign-ins, for example, sign-ins originating outside of Colorado. However, location is only one piece of the puzzle. You can further enhance this detection by incorporating additional identity signals that indicate a user’s behavior has changed. For example, you can look for sign-ins from countries where your organization has no presence, unfamiliar or unmanaged devices, unexpected operating systems or browsers, unusual user agents, or other authentication patterns that differ from a user’s normal activity. The query can be customized using attributes such as IP address, country, device OS platform, managed device status, device trust type, browser, user agent, and other available sign-in properties. Note: You may be wondering how the new EntraIdSignInEvents table differs from the familiar AADSignInEventsBeta table. Functionally, they contain the same sign-in data, with EntraIdSignInEvents serving as the successor to AADSignInEventsBeta. Microsoft plans to officially replace AADSignInEventsBeta with EntraIdSignInEvents on October 19, 2026. Use Case 5: One Alert Is Not the End of the Story — Detecting Mailbox Forwarding After a Security Alert A security alert is usually the beginning of an investigation, not the end. Once a user is flagged, security analysts need to answer a critical question: What did the attacker do next using this compromised identity? For example, what happens if the same user involved in a security alert creates a mailbox forwarding rule shortly afterward? This sequence of events may indicate an attacker attempting to establish persistence, maintain visibility, or continue collecting sensitive information after an initial compromise. By correlating Microsoft Defender XDR alert telemetry with mailbox forwarding activity, security teams can uncover suspicious follow-on actions. The KQL query shown below identifies a user who is flagged in a security alert then creates a mailbox forwarding rule within a defined time window. // This query identifies mailbox forwarding rules created after security alert let AlertedUsers = AlertEvidence | where isnotempty(AccountUpn) | summarize AlertTimestamp = min(Timestamp), AlertTitle = any(Title) by AlertId, User = AccountUpn; let MailForwardingEvents = CloudAppEvents | where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox") | extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData) | extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId) | extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters) | mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue) | extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue) | extend ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName, Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name), ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value), MailboxRuleTimestamp = Timestamp | where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" | where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@" | project MailboxRuleTimestamp, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP; AlertedUsers | join kind=inner MailForwardingEvents on User | where MailboxRuleTimestamp between (AlertTimestamp .. AlertTimestamp + 8h) | extend MinutesAfterAlert = datetime_diff("minute", MailboxRuleTimestamp, AlertTimestamp) | project AlertTimestamp, MailboxRuleTimestamp, MinutesAfterAlert, AlertId, AlertTitle, User, ActionType, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress | sort by AlertTimestamp asc For example, a suspicious sign-in alert was generated on 6/28 at 4:24 PM MT , and the same user created two mailbox forwarding rules that day after 11:00 PM MT , the query output brings these related events together. As shown in the following screenshot, the query output includes the alert details, mailbox forwarding timestamps, forwarding destinations, and other relevant metadata. When Attackers Hijack Your Inbox: Detecting Mailbox Forwarding Rules with Microsoft Defender XDR was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

The following screenshot shows the inbox redirect rule configuration.

In addition to creating an inbox rule, Outlook also allows you to enable mailbox forwarding, which automatically forwards all incoming messages to another email address.

On June 28, 2026, at 10:09 PM MT, I enabled mailbox forwarding by turning on “Enable forwarding” and configured all incoming messages to be forwarded to my personal Yahoo account, as shown in the following screenshot. Unlike inbox rules, mailbox forwarding configured this way does not have a rule name.

As I configured the different email forwarding settings, these activities were captured by Microsoft Purview Audit and became available in Defender Advanced Hunting in near real time. The following KQL query lists various mailbox forwarding rule creation events, including the three scenarios just described:

// This query lists mailbox forwarding rule creation events
CloudAppEvents
| where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox")
| extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId)
| extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters)
| mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue)
| extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue)
| extend
   ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName,
   Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name),
   ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value)
| where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" 
| where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@"
| project Timestamp, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP
| sort by Timestamp asc

As shown in the next screen capture, the query successfully identifies the three different types of mailbox forwarding scenarios that were just discussed.

Security Use Cases: Turning Mailbox Forwarding Telemetry into Actionable Detections

Detecting mailbox forwarding rules is a good starting point. The real power comes from connecting the dots across Microsoft Defender XDR telemetry to uncover attack patterns that may otherwise go unnoticed. By correlating mailbox forwarding activity with user risk, external destinations, identity signals, and existing security alerts, security teams can transform simple audit events into powerful behavioral detections.

Use Case 1: Detecting and Alerting on Mailbox Forwarding Rules Created for High-Risk Users

Attackers don’t always target random mailboxes. They often prioritize accounts with access to valuable information, such as executives, finance teams, legal departments, HR personnel, and security leaders. By creating mailbox forwarding rules on these high-value accounts, attackers can quietly monitor sensitive communications and collect intelligence while remaining unnoticed.

Security teams can reduce this risk by prioritizing mailbox forwarding activities involving high-risk users. By adding a user-based filter, the mailbox forwarding query introduced earlier can be easily customized to focus only on specific accounts that require additional monitoring. For example, the following filter limits the query to three predefined high-risk users:

| where User has_any ("axx@mycompany.com", "bxx@mycompany.com", "cxx@mycompany.com")

In a production environment, this list can be customized based on organization’s privileged accounts, executive users, sensitive business roles, or other identities requiring enhanced monitoring.

The complete updated query, including the high-risk user filter, is shown below:

// This query detects mailbox forwarding rules created for high-risk users
CloudAppEvents
| where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox")
| extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId)
| where User has_any ("axx@mycompany.com", "bxx@ mycompany.com", "cxx@mycompany.com")
| extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters)
| mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue)
| extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue)
| extend
   ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName,
   Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name),
   ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value)
| where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" 
| where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@"
| project Timestamp, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP
| sort by Timestamp asc
Operationalizing Threat Hunting with Custom Detection Rules

Threat hunting queries are valuable for investigating suspicious activity, but security teams can take it a step further by converting these queries into custom detection rules. This allows Microsoft Defender XDR to continuously run the KQL query in the background and automatically generate an alert when matching activity is detected.

As shown below, the “Create detection rule” option (highlighted in the red box) allows you to turn any hunting query into an automated detection.

The next screenshot shows the configuration experience for creating the custom detection rule.

Use Case 2: Detecting Multiple Mailboxes Forwarding to the Same External Email Address

A single mailbox forwarding rule set to an external address may be legitimate. However, multiple user mailboxes forwarding to the same external email address can be suspicious. This pattern may indicate a large-scale compromise, insider activity, or an attacker systematically collecting sensitive communications from multiple users.

KQL makes it easy to uncover this type of activity by aggregating mailbox forwarding events. The following query detects when three or more user mailboxes are configured to forward email to the same external email address.

// This query finds multiple mailboxes forwarding to the same external recipient
CloudAppEvents
| where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox")
| extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId)
| extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters)
| mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue)
| extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue)
| extend
   ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName,
   Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name),
   ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value)
| where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" 
| where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@" and ForwardingEmailAddress !endswith "@mycompany.com" // Change from mycompany.com to your own domain
| summarize
    Users = make_set(User),
    UserCount = dcount(User),
    RuleNames = make_set(ForwardingRuleName)
    by ForwardingEmailAddress
| where UserCount >= 3

In this query, the threshold is controlled by the following filter:

| where UserCount >= 3

You can easily adjust this value to suit your environment.

Additionally, to reduce noise, this query also excludes your organization’s email domain by using the following filter:

ForwardingEmailAddress !endswith "@mycompany.com"

Don’t forget to replace @mycompany.com with your organization’s email domain so the query focuses only on mail forwarded to external recipients.

Use Case 3: Detecting Mailbox Forwarding Rules to Specific External Domains

Security analysts are often interested in identifying unauthorized or suspicious email forwarding to external email services such as Gmail, Yahoo, and other personal email providers. This is more than just a compliance concern; these services are also common destinations for mailbox forwarding rules created by attackers. Monitoring forwarding activity to these domains provides a simple but effective way to detect potential Business Email Compromise and unauthorized data exfiltration.

The following query identifies mailbox forwarding rules configured to a predefined list of external domains, including Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook.com, and Proton Mail.

// This query finds mailbox forwarding rules set to specific external domains
CloudAppEvents
| where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox")
| extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId)
| extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters)
| mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue)
| extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue)
| extend
   ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName,
   Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name),
   ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value)
| where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" 
| where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@"
| where ForwardingEmailAddress has_any ("gmail.com", "yahoo.com", "outlook.com", "proton.me") // Customize this list by adding or removing external domains of interest
| project Timestamp, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP
| sort by Timestamp asc

Note, the external domain list in the KQL query is fully customizable. You can update the query filter by adding or removing domains based on the email services or destinations that are most relevant to your organization’s security monitoring needs.

Use Case 4: One Event is Interesting. Two Related Events Tell a Story. Correlating Suspicious Sign-ins with Mailbox Forwarding Rules

A mailbox forwarding rule by itself may not be enough to indicate malicious activity. However, when it is created shortly after a suspicious sign-in, the story becomes much more compelling. Instead of investigating mailbox activity in isolation, you can correlate mailbox forwarding telemetry with suspicious Microsoft Entra ID sign-in events to uncover post-compromise persistence commonly seen in Business Email Compromise attacks.

The EntraIdSignInEvents table in Defender Advanced Hunting contains Microsoft Entra ID sign-in events, including sign-ins to Microsoft 365 and other applications authenticated through Entra ID. It also provides additional identity context, such as device name, IP address, geographic location, and session details. This allows the identification of unusual or suspicious sign-in activity. By combining this information with mailbox forwarding events, security teams can identify suspicious behavioral sequences rather than isolated events.

For example, the user, as shown below, normally signs in from Denver, Colorado using a registered device named FamilyPC1. This user consistently accesses resources through the Microsoft Edge browser with the same user agent. However, as seen from the screenshot below, one sign-in event stands out. It originates from Cheyenne, Wyoming, using a different browser, is not associated with a registered device, and contains no user agent information.

This suspicious sign-in becomes even more interesting when it is followed by a mailbox forwarding event involving the same user account. The following KQL query correlates such suspicious Entra ID sign-ins with subsequent mailbox forwarding rule creation to identify those potential attack patterns.

// This query identifies suspicious sign-in followed by the creation of a mail forwarding rule
let SuspiciousSignIns =
EntraIdSignInEvents
| where State != "Colorado"
| where Application == "Office 365 Exchange Online"
| extend User = AccountUpn, SignInTime = Timestamp, UserSignInIP = IPAddress
| project SignInTime, User, UserSignInIP, Country, State, City, Application, LogonType, DeviceName, OSPlatform, DeviceTrustType, IsManaged, Browser, UserAgent;
let MailForwarding =
CloudAppEvents
| where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox")
| extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId), ForwardTime = Timestamp
| extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters)
| mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue)
| extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue)
| extend
   ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName,
   Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name),
   ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value)
| where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" 
| where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@"
| project ForwardTime, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP;
SuspiciousSignIns
| join kind=inner MailForwarding on User
| where ForwardTime between (SignInTime .. SignInTime + 1d)
| project
    SignInTime,
    ForwardTime,
    TimeToForwardRule = ForwardTime - SignInTime,
    User, UserSignInIP, Country, State, City, Application, LogonType, DeviceName, OSPlatform, DeviceTrustType, IsManaged, Browser, UserAgent,
    ActionType, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress
| sort by SignInTime asc, ForwardTime asc

Using the events from the previous three test scenarios along with the suspicious Entra ID sign-in discussed earlier, this query connects the dots across multiple security signals and brings the entire attack sequence together in a single query output. It identifies an unusual sign-in from Wyoming, followed by the creation of multiple mailbox forwarding rules, allowing analysts to see the related activities and timeline in one view.

The next two screenshots highlight different portions of the KQL query output. The first screenshot shows the beginning of the results, while the second displays a later section of the output.

This KQL query uses geographic deviation as the signal to identify potentially suspicious sign-ins, for example, sign-ins originating outside of Colorado. However, location is only one piece of the puzzle. You can further enhance this detection by incorporating additional identity signals that indicate a user’s behavior has changed.

For example, you can look for sign-ins from countries where your organization has no presence, unfamiliar or unmanaged devices, unexpected operating systems or browsers, unusual user agents, or other authentication patterns that differ from a user’s normal activity. The query can be customized using attributes such as IP address, country, device OS platform, managed device status, device trust type, browser, user agent, and other available sign-in properties.

Note: You may be wondering how the new EntraIdSignInEvents table differs from the familiar AADSignInEventsBeta table. Functionally, they contain the same sign-in data, with EntraIdSignInEvents serving as the successor to AADSignInEventsBeta. Microsoft plans to officially replace AADSignInEventsBeta with EntraIdSignInEvents on October 19, 2026.

Use Case 5: One Alert Is Not the End of the Story — Detecting Mailbox Forwarding After a Security Alert

A security alert is usually the beginning of an investigation, not the end. Once a user is flagged, security analysts need to answer a critical question: What did the attacker do next using this compromised identity?

For example, what happens if the same user involved in a security alert creates a mailbox forwarding rule shortly afterward? This sequence of events may indicate an attacker attempting to establish persistence, maintain visibility, or continue collecting sensitive information after an initial compromise.

By correlating Microsoft Defender XDR alert telemetry with mailbox forwarding activity, security teams can uncover suspicious follow-on actions. The KQL query shown below identifies a user who is flagged in a security alert then creates a mailbox forwarding rule within a defined time window.

// This query identifies mailbox forwarding rules created after security alert
let AlertedUsers =
AlertEvidence
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn)
| summarize
    AlertTimestamp = min(Timestamp),
    AlertTitle = any(Title)
    by AlertId, User = AccountUpn;
let MailForwardingEvents =
CloudAppEvents
| where ActionType has_any ("New-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox")
| extend ParsedData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend User = tostring(ParsedData.UserId)
| extend ParameterValue = tostring(ParsedData.Parameters)
| mv-expand parsejson(ParameterValue)
| extend ParameterJson = parse_json(ParameterValue)
| extend
   ForwardingRuleName = ObjectName,
   Action = tostring(ParameterJson.Name),
   ForwardingEmailAddress = tostring(ParameterJson.Value),
   MailboxRuleTimestamp = Timestamp
| where Action contains "forward" or Action contains "redirect" 
| where ForwardingEmailAddress contains "@"
| project MailboxRuleTimestamp, ActionType, Application, Action, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress, User, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP;
AlertedUsers
| join kind=inner MailForwardingEvents on User
| where MailboxRuleTimestamp between (AlertTimestamp .. AlertTimestamp + 8h)
| extend MinutesAfterAlert = datetime_diff("minute", MailboxRuleTimestamp, AlertTimestamp)
| project AlertTimestamp, MailboxRuleTimestamp, MinutesAfterAlert, AlertId, AlertTitle, User, ActionType, ForwardingRuleName, ForwardingEmailAddress
| sort by AlertTimestamp asc

For example, a suspicious sign-in alert was generated on 6/28 at 4:24 PM MT, and the same user created two mailbox forwarding rules that day after 11:00 PM MT, the query output brings these related events together. As shown in the following screenshot, the query output includes the alert details, mailbox forwarding timestamps, forwarding destinations, and other relevant metadata.

When Attackers Hijack Your Inbox: Detecting Mailbox Forwarding Rules with Microsoft Defender XDR was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Attackers Don’t Need Your Devices Anymore They Just Need Your Identity.
items.summary: The Silent Lateral Move You’re Not Seeing Your EDR watches every endpoint. But modern attackers have learned to move between identities instead of devices. The good news is that the telemetry for every step of this movement exists across your hunting tables. The trick is knowing which table holds which evidence and how to correlate across them. Let me show you a real-world attack path that many SOC teams still miss. Sarah in accounts payable clicks a DocuSign link in a phishing email. She enters her credentials on a fake login page that relays everything in real time to Microsoft. She completes MFA and the attacker steals her session token after login. Her laptop is still clean, her password still works and nothing has been installed. Now the attacker has Sarah’s cloud identity. But they do not touch her device. Instead, they use her token to make Graph API calls like GET /users, GET /groups, GET /directoryRoles and GET /applications. In other words, they map the tenant and look for valuable access. After that, they do something more dangerous. Using Sarah’s token, they register a new app in Entra ID, give it a boring name like SP-Migration-Helper-Prod, create a client secret and add Mail.Read and Mail.Send permissions. In many tenants, this is possible because users are allowed to register apps and consent to permissions by default. Sarah is not an admin, but the attacker does not need her to be one. Now the attacker has a second identity a service principal. It has no device, no MFA and no conditional access. It only needs a secret to authenticate and it can read mailboxes. They use it to read the CFO’s email, find a wire transfer thread and reply with updated banking details. The message comes from the CFO’s mailbox through Graph API, so it looks legitimate and passes SPF and DKIM checks. That is how the money disappears. Three identities were involved:- Sarah, the malicious service principal and the CFO. No device was compromised after the initial phishing attack. Every step was logged somewhere in your data, but most SOC teams do not yet have the correlation logic to connect the dots. Why this attack needs its own detection Traditional lateral movement usually happens between devices. Think PSExec, RDP or WMI. In those cases, you normally see process activity on the target machine and network traffic between endpoints, so EDR tools are built to catch that well. But this attack is different. It moves between identities instead of devices. Sarah’s identity leads to a service principal and then that service principal is used to access David’s mailbox. After the phishing click, no device is involved. The good news is that the telemetry is available in you Defender XDR. MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs can show the API enumeration, CloudAppEvents can show the app registration, permission changes and mailbox access and IdentityLogonEvents can show the authentication activity. The challenge is connecting those signals together so the full attack becomes visible. The identity-plane kill chain To detect this kind of attack, it helps to break it into stages. Each stage leaves different clues in different tables. Stage 1: Identity compromise The attacker takes over a user account through phishing or token theft. At this point, everything happens through cloud authentication. You may see unusual sign-ins in IdentityLogonEvents and AADSignInEventsBeta, such as new IPs, strange locations, Anomalous Token or logins to apps the user does not normally use. Stage 2: Permission discovery Next, the attacker uses that account to look around the tenant through Graph API. They enumerate users, groups, roles, applications and service principals. This is like scanning the environment without touching endpoints. You can see this in MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs as GET requests to enumeration endpoints. Stage 3: Pivot Then the attacker creates a new non-human identity, such as a new app registration or adds credentials to an existing service principal. After that, they grant it access to resources they want to target. The evidence usually appears in CloudAppEvents, with actions like adding an application, adding service principal credentials or assigning app roles. Stage 4: Cross-identity access Now the attacker uses the service principal to access data that belongs to other users who were never directly compromised. That may include mailbox access or file downloads. In CloudAppEvents this often shows up as AccountType = "Application" and in MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs as requests to endpoints like /users/{id}/messages from a ServicePrincipalId. Stage 5: Action on objective Finally, the attacker uses that access to send fraudulent emails, steal data or create more identities for persistence. You can usually see this across CloudAppEvents and EmailEvents. How to correlate data across the kill chain: To catch this attack, you need to follow the trail across multiple tables. The first step is to spot directory enumeration in MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs. When an attacker is exploring the tenant, they usually send many GET requests to different endpoints in a short time. Normal apps usually keep hitting the same few endpoints, but an attacker is trying to map the environment quickly. Microsoft’s Graph activity logs are designed to give you that API-level visibility. 1.Detecting directory enumeration through Graph API This is where MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs becomes critical. When an attacker enumerates your directory, they make GET requests to multiple resource endpoints in a short window. Legitimate applications tend to hit one or two endpoints repeatedly. An attacker doing reconnaissance hits many different endpoints quickly. Focus on users not service principals: As a Best practice build a baseline of which AppIds normally query which endpoints. Most legitimate applications have a narrow, consistent pattern. An AppId suddenly querying endpoints it has never touched before or a UserId making direct Graph calls through tools like Graph Explorer or PowerShell should trigger review. let ReconEndpoints = dynamic(["users", "groups", "directoryRoles","applications", "servicePrincipals","roleManagement", "organization","devices", "oauth2PermissionGrants","administrativeUnits"]); MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where RequestMethod == "GET" | where ResponseStatusCode == 200 | where isnotempty(UserId) and isempty(ServicePrincipalId) | extend ParsedPath = tostring(parse_url(RequestUri).Path) | extend CleanPath = tolower(replace_string(replace_string(ParsedPath, "//", "/"),"v1.0/", "")) | extend CleanPath = replace_string(CleanPath, "beta/", "") | extend GraphResource = tostring(split(CleanPath, "/")[1]) | where GraphResource in (ReconEndpoints) | summarize TotalRequests = count(), UniqueEndpoints = dcount(GraphResource), EndpointsHit = make_set(GraphResource), TotalResponseSize = sum(ResponseSizeBytes), DistinctAppIds = dcount(AppId), AppsUsed = make_set(AppId), FirstRequest = min(TimeGenerated), LastRequest = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | where UniqueEndpoints >= 4 and TotalRequests > 50 Look for the attacker tooling signature: Tools like AzureHound, ROADtools and GraphRunner hit a very specific combination of high-value recon endpoints in rapid succession. Narrow the endpoint list to the ones that matter most for attack path mapping and raise the threshold. let HighValueRecon = dynamic([ "servicePrincipals", "applications", "directoryRoles", "roleManagement", "oauth2PermissionGrants"]); MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where RequestMethod == "GET" | where ResponseStatusCode == 200 | extend ParsedPath = tostring(parse_url(RequestUri).Path) | extend CleanPath = tolower(replace_string(replace_string(ParsedPath, "//", "/"),"v1.0/", "")) | extend CleanPath = replace_string(CleanPath, "beta/", "") | extend GraphResource = tostring(split(CleanPath, "/")[1]) | where GraphResource in (HighValueRecon) | extend ActorId = coalesce(UserId, ServicePrincipalId) | summarize TotalRequests = count(), UniqueEndpoints = dcount(GraphResource), EndpointsHit = make_set(GraphResource), TotalResponseSize = sum(ResponseSizeBytes) by ActorId, AppId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | where UniqueEndpoints >= 3 2.Enriching recon detection with sign-in context (Stage 1 to Stage 2 correlation) When the enumeration query returns a suspicious UserId, cross-reference it with authentication data to see if the identity was recently compromised or any risky sign-in patterns observed. let ReconEndpoints = dynamic(["users", "groups", "directoryRoles","applications", "servicePrincipals","roleManagement", "organization","devices", "oauth2PermissionGrants"]); let SuspectUsers =MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where RequestMethod == "GET" | where ResponseStatusCode == 200 | where isnotempty(UserId) and isempty(ServicePrincipalId) | extend ParsedPath = tostring(parse_url(RequestUri).Path) | extend GraphResource = tostring(split(replace_string(replace_string(tolower(ParsedPath),"v1.0/", ""), "beta/", ""), "/")[1]) | where GraphResource in (ReconEndpoints) | summarize UniqueEndpoints = dcount(GraphResource), RequestCount = count(), EndpointsHit = make_set(GraphResource), TotalResponseBytes = sum(ResponseSizeBytes) by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | where UniqueEndpoints >= 4 | distinct UserId; SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where UserId in (SuspectUsers) | where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("medium", "high") or RiskState == "atRisk" | project TimeGenerated,UserPrincipalName,IPAddress,Location,AppDisplayName,RiskLevelDuringSignIn,RiskState,RiskEventTypes_V2,AuthenticationRequirement,ConditionalAccessStatus If the same identity shows a sign-in from an unusual IP followed by a burst of Graph API enumeration within a few hours, you have strong evidence of stages 1 and 2 happening in sequence. 3.Detecting identity pivots through app registration (Stage 3) Run this regularly and maintain a baseline of which accounts normally register applications. In most organizations that list should be short and limited to IT administrators. Any account outside that baseline registering an app or adding credentials to a service principal deserves immediate investigation. CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType in ( "Add application.", "Add service principal.", "Add service principal credentials.", "Update application - Certificates and secrets management ", "Add app role assignment to service principal.", "Consent to application.", "Add delegated permission grant.") | where AccountType != "Application" | project Timestamp, ActorAccount = AccountDisplayName,ActorUPN = AccountId,ActionType,TargetApp = tostring(RawEventData.Target[0].ID),TargetAppName = tostring(RawEventData.Target[1].ID) If above query brings High False Positives then Detect attack chain sequences not individual events: Instead of alerting on every single action, look for users who performed multiple distinct actions in a short window. A legitimate admin might do one of these actions in isolation. An attacker building a pivot does three or more within an hour. let AdminRoles = dynamic(["Global Administrator","Application Administrator","Cloud Application Administrator","Privileged Role Administrator"]); let KnownAdmins = IdentityInfo | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where AssignedRoles has_any (AdminRoles) | distinct AccountUpn; CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType has_any( "Add application", "Add service principal", "Add service principal credentials", "Update application - Certificates and secrets management", "Add app role assignment to service principal", "Consent to application", "Add delegated permission grant") | where AccountType != "Application" | extend UserID=tostring(RawEventData.UserId) | summarize EventCount = count(), DistinctActions = dcount(ActionType), ActionSequence = make_list(ActionType), TargetApps = make_set(tostring(RawEventData.Target[0].ID)), TargetAppNames = make_set(tostring(RawEventData.Target[1].ID)), FirstEvent = min(Timestamp), LastEvent = max(Timestamp) by UserID, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h) | extend DurationMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', LastEvent, FirstEvent) | extend IsAdmin = UserID in (KnownAdmins) | where (IsAdmin == false and DistinctActions >= 3) | project FirstEvent,LastEvent,DurationMinutes,ActorUPN = UserID,ActorAccount = AccountDisplayName,IsAdmin,DistinctActions,EventCount,ActionSequence,TargetApps,TargetAppNames Detecting credential drops on dormant service principals (Stage 3 variant): This query looks for service principals that had no Microsoft Graph activity for the last 30 days but suddenly got new credentials. In a normal environment, active apps usually make Graph API calls as part of their regular use. So if a service principal has been quiet for a long time and then gets new credentials, that is suspicious. It may mean someone is preparing a dormant identity for abuse. The query checks inactivity from two sides: the service principal itself did not make Graph API calls and no one accessed it through Graph API either. If both are true and credentials were just added, the query highlights the event and shows who added them and which service principal was targeted. //Get credential additions and extract both SP IDs let CredentialAdds = CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType has_any ("Add service principal credentials","Certificates and secrets") | extend Targets = tostring(RawEventData.Target) | extend TargetSPId = extract(@'ServicePrincipal_([0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12})',1, Targets) | extend TargetSPName = extract( @'"Type"\s*:\s*1[^}]*"Name"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"', 1, Targets) | where isnotempty(TargetSPId) | summarize arg_min(Timestamp, *) by ReportId, TargetSPId | project CredAddTime = Timestamp,ActorUPN = AccountId,ActorAccount = AccountDisplayName,AccountType,ActionType,TargetSPId, TargetSPName; // SPs that made Graph calls in last 30 days (as caller) let ActiveCallers =MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where isnotempty(ServicePrincipalId) | distinct ServicePrincipalId; //SPs that were referenced in Graph API URLs in last 30 days let ActiveTargets =MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where RequestUri has "servicePrincipals/" | extend ReferencedSPId = extract(@'servicePrincipals/([0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12})',1, RequestUri) | where isnotempty(ReferencedSPId) | distinct ReferencedSPId; // Flag credential adds where SP had zero Graph activity CredentialAdds | extend WasActiveCaller = TargetSPId in (ActiveCallers),WasActiveTarget = TargetSPId in (ActiveTargets) | extend HasAnyGraphActivity =WasActiveCaller or WasActiveTarget | where HasAnyGraphActivity == false | project CredAddTime,ActorUPN,ActorAccount,AccountType,ActionType,TargetSPId,TargetSPName 4.Detecting non-human identities accessing user resources This query looks for application identities that had no history of accessing Exchange, SharePoint or OneDrive in the last 23 days, but suddenly started doing so in the last 7 days. It flags cases where the app touched 3 or more user resources or made 20 or more access calls in a single hour. In a normal environment, legitimate apps like email archivers or DLP tools usually show steady activity over time. If an app appears for the first time and immediately starts reading mailboxes, downloading files or accessing SharePoint sites, it should be checked.
